page_title: Don’t Let Architecture Astronauts Scare You

sources.entry: Don’t Let Architecture Astronauts Scare You, Joel

summary.title: Don't Let Architecture Astronauts Scare You
summary.one_liner: Joel Spolsky's essay warns that over-abstracted "architecture astronauts" chase grand designs and hype while missing the practical problems users actually need solved.
takeaways: Going too far up the abstraction ladder (e.g. from file sending to generic 'messaging') can produce vague ideas that mean little.
Architecture astronauts focus on architecture (such as peer-to-peer) and overlook the feature users actually value, like finding and playing a song by name.
New architectures and technologies are often hyped as solving big problems, but many offer little beyond what earlier technologies (DCOM, CORBA, JavaBeans) already did.
Judge a technology by whether it lets you do something new that you could not do before, rather than by its architectural elegance or marketing.
summary.summary: This 2001 essay by Joel Spolsky is an opinion piece rather than a tutorial. It describes "architecture astronauts": engineers who climb too high in abstraction and become fixated on grand architectures. He illustrates the point with Napster (where the useful feature was simple search and playback, not peer-to-peer), and with hype around Java, XML/SOAP, Microsoft .NET and Hailstorm, and Sun Jini. The argument is that such architectures often reimplement older ideas and that the real test is whether they solve a useful problem.
